lesson.title: Testing the Difference Within: The Paired T-Test
lesson.summary: Once paired data has been collapsed into a single list of differences, the paired t-test is simply a one-sample t-test performed on those differences, almost always testing whether the mean difference is zero.
lesson.body:
Paired data reduces two columns of numbers into one column of differences, d, as shown in paired data. Once that reduction is done, there is no new formula to learn: the paired t-test is the one-sample t-test applied to the d-values. The test statistic is t equals (xbar_d minus mu_d0) divided by (s_d divided by the square root of n), with degrees of freedom n minus 1, where n is the number of pairs. The hypothesized value mu_d0 is almost always 0, representing no average change or no average difference between the members of a pair.

Continuing the weight loss example: n equals 6 pairs, xbar_d equals 4.5, s_d equals about 2.074. The hypotheses are H0: mu_d equals 0 (the program produces no average weight change) against Ha: mu_d is greater than 0 (the program produces average weight loss). The standard error of the mean difference is s_d divided by the square root of n, which is 2.074 divided by the square root of 6, or 2.074 divided by 2.449, about 0.847. The test statistic is 4.5 divided by 0.847, about 5.32. Degrees of freedom is 6 minus 1 equals 5. Checking the t-table at df equals 5, the critical value for a one-tailed area of 0.005 is 4.032, and for a one-tailed area of 0.001 it is 5.893. Our statistic, 5.32, falls between those two values, so the p-value is between 0.001 and 0.005, extremely small. We reject H0 at any conventional significance level and conclude there is strong evidence the program produces real average weight loss, not just random fluctuation.

The conditions to check are the same ones from the one-sample t-test, just applied to the differences rather than the original measurements: the pairs (not the individual measurements) should arise from a random sample or random assignment, the differences from different pairs should be independent of each other (one person's weight change should not influence another's), and the differences themselves should look roughly normal, or n should be large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to compensate, exactly the tradeoff explored in the upcoming robustness section. With only 6 pairs here, it is worth glancing at the six differences, 4, 3, 7, 2, 7, 4, to check that nothing looks like a wild outlier or strong skew before trusting the result.

It is worth pausing on how little is actually new here. The formula, the degrees of freedom rule, and the whole logic of the test are identical to the one-sample t-test already covered. The only genuinely new skill is recognizing that the data were paired in the first place and reducing them to differences before doing anything else, which is precisely the judgment call formalized next.
